questions.q: In the gatekeeper model described in this lesson, what does the DBA do for every database change?
options: Manually reviews and approves it by hand before it reaches production
Automatically approves it without looking, trusting developers
Deletes it and asks the developer to resubmit
Runs it directly in production without any review
questions.explain: The gatekeeper model is defined by a DBA personally reviewing and signing off on each change one at a time.

questions.q: Why does the gatekeeper model break down as deployment frequency increases?
options: The DBA becomes a single point of contention that every change has to queue behind
SQL Server stops allowing more than one deployment per month
It doesn't break down — it works equally well at any frequency
Developers are legally required to wait for quarterly releases
questions.explain: One person manually reviewing every change can't keep pace once a team wants to ship many times a week.

questions.q: What does the enabler model replace manual per-change review with?
options: Automated guardrails, like CI checks and IaC templates, that enforce standards on every change
No review process of any kind
A rotating on-call schedule of junior developers doing the review instead
A requirement that all changes be submitted in writing to management
questions.explain: The enabler model moves the DBA's judgment into automated checks that run on every change without a human bottleneck.

questions.q: According to this lesson, what stays exactly the same for the DBA under the enabler model?
options: The DBA remains the accountable expert on safety, performance, and recoverability
The DBA no longer has any responsibility for data integrity
The DBA now reports to the development team instead of IT
The DBA's job becomes purely clerical, with no technical judgment involved
questions.explain: DevOps relocates when the DBA's judgment is applied — it doesn't remove that judgment or the accountability behind it.

questions.q: In the CI guardrail example in this lesson, what does the pipeline step check for before allowing a migration to merge?
options: Whether the migration script contains a destructive statement like DROP COLUMN or DROP TABLE without an approval tag
Whether the developer's name starts with a vowel
Whether the migration script is written in T-SQL rather than PowerShell
Whether the staging server has more than 50% free disk space
questions.explain: The example guardrail blocks destructive statements unless they carry an explicit @approved-by-dba tag, catching risky changes automatically.
